subject: barnstormerBiplane
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: barnstormer biplane.
Style: whimsical.
reasoning:
I'm planning a whimsical biplane model, structuring it with a root body joint and separate hinge joints for the propeller, rudder, elevators, and ailerons, roughly sized like a classic Stearman barnstormer.

Setting up the hinge-style joints with the fuselage root, then picking a limited color palette and defining the fuselage loft stations with widths and heights from nose to tail...

Writing fuselage loft...

Still defining wing geometry...

2.55, with cabane struts rising from the fuselage top to meet it, giving a gap of about 1.5 and a slightly whimsical wing thickness. I'm adding ailerons as separate contrasting-colored extrude pieces on the upper wingtips, each hinged at a joint near the trailing edge aimed outward along the span.

I'll make ailerons sit slightly proud of the wing by giving them a bit more thickness (0.15 vs 0.12) so coplanar surfaces don't z-fight, painting them red for visibility. I'm also thinking about adding a roundel decal on the wings via an SVG texture for a fun decorative touch.

Since both fuselage decals project outward toward the viewer and up stays as world y, I don't think mirroring is needed for either side. For the wings, instead of decals I'll paint colored regions directly using a position-based color function, making the wingtips red against a cream base to keep texel density simpler.

With wings totaling roughly 50 square meters of painted area, the texel density works out to about 8mm resolution, which is fine. I'll add the tip coloring plus a thin yellow band between the red tip and cream body for a sunburst trim effect, then move on to the interplane struts, placing rods connecting the lower wing's top surface to the upper wing's bottom surface in the typical N-strut arrangement at symmetric x-offsets.

I'll simplify to one interplane strut pair per side plus the diagonal X-bracing wires connecting struts, and add long wires from the cabane to the lower wing strut base to tie the whole structure together.

Now I'm working out the cabane strut geometry, running V-shaped struts from the fuselage top up to the front and rear spars of the upper wing's center section, leaving a gap for the pilot's cockpit view underneath.

For whimsy, I'm considering adding a pilot with helmet and streaming scarf in the rear cockpit and a small goggled dog in the front cockpit, then adding a dark inset ellipse to the fuselage top to suggest the cockpit opening.

Since the loft section dimensions aren't fully known, I'll query the surface directly with a downward ray at the cockpit z-location to find the top hit point and use that to place the cockpit rim and sunken disc accurately.

Actually a simpler approach: sweep a closed catmull curve around an ellipse at the cockpit's top edge using leather material, rather than a torus. I'm computing ellipse points around the hit point with radius .32 in x and .42 in z, but realizing the fuselage surface curves downward away from center, so the ring needs to follow that drop rather than sit at constant height.

For the ring to hug the sloped surface, I'll drape the path onto the surface geometry so points snap to the nearest surface position, then sweep that draped path for the cockpit rim. For the dark cockpit opening, I'll skip the stick cylinder and instead use a slightly oversized flat disc embedded into the surface so its edges get buried under the rim.

Now I'm planning the pilot figure seated in the rear cockpit: a brown leather jacket torso capsule, skin-toned head sphere, a helmet cap, goggles made from cylinders with a strap, and a red-and-white scarf streaming backward.

For the scarf I want it to wave using a catmull-rom sweep from the neck backward with a flattened elliptical radius profile, and I'm giving the pilot a raised waving arm as a capsule from shoulder to an upward-outward point -- just plain geometric parts since this is a vehicle, not a creature needing joints.

For the front cockpit dog, I'm sketching a tan head sphere, snout box, nose, hanging ear ellipsoids, goggles, and a pink tongue, sized so only the head and chest show above the rim. I'm now second-guessing the z-positioning of the cockpits relative to the wings -- the pilot sits beyond the wing's trailing edge while a real Stearman has both cockpits tucked under the wing, so I'm considering shifting the upper and lower wing centers backward to fix the spacing.

I'm reworking the fuselage layout: nose and cowling around z=2.2-2.3, wings centered near z=0.3-0.55 with a 1.5 chord, dog cockpit at z≈-0.55 just behind the trailing edge, and pilot at z≈-1.45 with 0.9m spacing between cockpits, checking that the pilot's head height clears nothing above it. I'm defining fuselage cross-section stations from nose to tail tip, specifying y-center, width, and height at each z position, then starting the cowling as a lathed shape around the nose.

Designing the radial engine cowling as a lathe profile with a bulging radius, plus a bright front ring and a circular arrangement of small cylinders to mimic the visible engine cylinder heads poking out around the nose.

Though actually the cowling front cap should cover that area, so I'll simplify: add a flat front nose cap around z=2.35–2.5 for the hub and propeller, with the cylinder head ring treated as a tilted band near the front rather than radial stubs.

Actually, I'll give the plane some whimsy instead — a small dark intake ring on the cowling front mouth, plus googly eyes seated on the cowling's upper-front sides (flattened white spheres with black pupils) and a curved dark grille arc below the hub to suggest a smile.

Placing the eyes symmetrically on the front face above the hub, small white spheres offset from center, close enough to the hub but not overlapping it.

Now I'm checking that the cowling radius stays larger than the fuselage's half-width where they meet, so the nose cone reads as a distinct, slightly bulging shape rather than sinking into the body.

Working out the landing gear next: struts dropping from the fuselage underside to wheel hubs, with each wheel built as a lathed torus around the x-axis so the tire profile stays symmetric and the hub sits at the right height off the ground.

Setting up the wheel joints so they rotate along the outward axis, checking that the tire's lowest point touches ground level at y=0. I'm reconsidering the proportions to make the wheels chunkier and whimsical, bumping radius up to 0.6, and now working out the gear strut positions connecting fuselage to wheel hubs.

Now I'm adding an axle rod spanning between the two hubs and sketching a small tailwheel or skid near the tail, positioning it so it sits flush with the tail fuselage's lower edge.

I'm also working out the vertical fin as an extruded profile near the tail end, defining its forward-up outline points relative to an anchor point along the fuselage.

Working out the rudder as a separate hinged piece at the tail, defining its rounded outline relative to the hinge joint and setting colors—yellow for the rudder, red for the fin.

Now I'm placing the horizontal stabilizer, extruding it in the horizontal plane near the tail hinge with a rounded outline spanning about 1.25 units each side.

Then I'm defining two elevator joints near the stabilizer hinge, one on each side with opposite rotation directions, before extruding them outward.

Defining the fixed stabilizer outline so it butts against the elevator at the hinge line, then adding thin metal brace wires from the stab tips up to the fin top, and setting up the propeller joint position and orientation.

Now I'm shaping the two-blade propeller as a tapered paddle outline through the hub, tilting its orientation slightly so the blades read as angled rather than flat-vertical.

I'm checking propeller clearance and sizing the spinner cone, placing it at the hub with a lathe-generated outline and positioning the blades just behind it with proper thickness.

Then I'm adding a prop bone for rigging and moving to design curved exhaust pipes extending from the cowling sides.

Now I'm thinking about the upper wing section and considering adding small windscreens in front of each cockpit, trying a simple translucent light-blue slab shape for them since the materials are opaque only.

For decorating the fuselage, I want to add a number decal or roundel star using SVG text and shapes, maybe a "7" with bold styling and a star emblem.

Reconsidering placement though—the fuselage near the tail is too narrow for a good-sized roundel, so instead I'll place decals flat on the wing surfaces (top and bottom) using appropriate position and orientation vectors.

"BARNSTORM" won't fit, so I'll go simpler—a round badge with "7" placed on the fuselage side for a readable emblem. For extra flair, I'll add a trailing scarf from the pilot and small triangular pennants at the wing tips rather than a heavy towed banner.

Now I'm working out a paint function for wing rib stripes, coloring bands by distance from center into red, yellow, and cream tones to suggest rib lines across the wing surface.

For the fuselage, I'm sketching a similar paint approach using position and normal to add a yellow band near the tail and cream shading beneath, maybe with a chevron accent near the cowling.

I'm adding small detail pieces: a leather headrest hump as a scaled sphere behind the pilot, a decorative cream/yellow fuel dome on the upper wing center section, and refining strut placements for visual interest.

Now I'm building out the pilot figure itself — torso as a capsule, head as a small skin-colored sphere, a leather helmet cap shaped as a partial sphere, and goggles made from small cylinders for the lenses with dark metal rims and light blue lens color.

Positioning the pilot's nose and adding a whimsical handlebar moustache with curling catmull-rom points below the nose for a barnstormer look.

I'm checking that the moustache coordinates stay outside the head sphere's surface, recalculating the sphere's z-depth at each point so the moustache doesn't clip into the face.

Now I'm reusing that helper for the nose, moustache, and goggles, placing goggles near the head center, then positioning the arms: one raised and waving with a mitten hand, the other bent forward gripping a control stick near the cockpit.

For the scarf, I'm defining a curved path trailing back from the neck using several control points, then sweeping a flat ribbon shape along that curve with alternating red and cream stripe colors for a candy-cane effect.

Now I'm placing the dog in the front cockpit facing forward — building a tan head sphere, a snout box, a small black nose, and two floppy ear ellipsoids positioned on either side of the head.

Checking the dog's position relative to the windscreen and pilot's cockpit—dog snout clears the windscreen edge, and the spacing between dog and pilot cockpits looks consistent with the windscreen tucked behind the dog's back. Now I'm thinking about adding small pennant flags on the upper wing tips, mounted on vertical rods.

Writing pennant shape...

I'm also laying out the joint hierarchy—fuselage as root, with propeller, rudder, elevators, ailerons, wheels, and tailwheel all parented to it, and positioning the aileron joints.

Working out wing geometry...

Working out the aileron outline coordinates with chamfered corners, checking that the trailing edge point matches up with the wing's chord geometry at x=3.95.

I'm thinking the aileron can overlap the wing slightly since it's thicker, painted red against the cream wing. Now I'm defining the rotation geometry for mirrored ailerons, setting hinge axes aligned with the wing's spanwise bone direction from the fuselage root.

Setting up the wing extrusion with the correct orientation and thickness axis, making sure each part references its bone explicitly rather than relying on nearest-joint inference. I'm also tallying the color palette constants to stay under the limit, then starting on SVG textures.

Writing roundel and badge SVGs...

I need to get the fuselage surface for raycasting cockpit heights, guarding against null hits. For landing gear, I'm sizing strut rods with thin metal radii for the legs and wood-colored interplane struts, defining the rod geometry signature next.

Rod calls take endpoints, radius, color, and a bone reference; I'll pass the fuselage bone explicitly for stability. For wheels, I'm building lathe profiles for the tire and hub cap, setting the tire outline symmetric around the axle axis and a thin yellow hubcap profile layered on top.

Now I'm checking clearances — tires and tail wheel both touch y=0 as the lowest points. I'm sketching a small lathe profile for the tail wheel and planning a rod strut to connect it to the tail.

Working through the overall height budget, I decide the pennant masts should be scaled down to 0.4 to avoid dominating the bounding box, and I'm adding whimsical cowling "eye" details for character. Now I'm setting up the imports and builder utilities needed to start writing the actual scene code.

Defining joints and roles...

Settling on a plane palette for a barnstormer look: red fuselage, cream wings, and now deciding between yellow or teal for the cowling and spinner, leaning toward yellow cowling with teal accents on struts and spinner.

Now I'm placing the eyes as protruding spheres on the cowling face, with small black pupils and tilted dark eyebrow capsules above each to give it an expressive character.

Checking if brows push past the face boundary at that radius, I decide to adjust eye position lower instead to keep proportions tidy. Then I work out the smile curve endpoints and confirm they stay within the face radius, leaving the center hub spinner radius for later.

I'm checking eye overlap with the spinner base and adjusting positions slightly, shrinking the spinner radius a bit for clearance, then moving on to pupil placement and the propeller blade tilt and spin setup.

Now I'm working out the cabane strut and interplane positions, making sure the front and rear spars line up correctly between the lower and upper wing centers given the wing thickness.

Still adding bracing wires...

I'm checking the horizontal stabilizer position against the fuselage cross-section at that station, confirming it sits centered within the fuselage height, and verifying the fin base aligns properly with the fuselage top before placing the rudder joint at the fin's trailing edge.

Now I'm working out a helper function that casts a ray downward from above the fuselage surface to find the top skin height at any given z-position, which I'll use to properly seat the cockpit canopy discs against the fuselage contour rather than guessing at fixed heights.

I'm trying different placements for the dark coaming disc relative to the fuselage surface height, but the geometry keeps hiding it inside the body or leaving it floating oddly at the edges — none of these height offsets create a visible cockpit opening, so I need a different approach that actually carves out space rather than just layering a disc on top.

Instead I'll build the coaming as an actual lathe-shaped wall: a short cylindrical rim that extends from below the fuselage surface up to just above it, forming a raised collar the dark disc can sit inside, rather than trying to place a flat disc at some magic height.

Simplifying my approach, I'll switch to using two cylinders instead of a lathe geometry: an outer leather-colored cylinder for the rim and a smaller dark disc cylinder positioned slightly higher to create a recessed ring effect at the top.

Adjusting the windscreen outline to droop down and anchor onto the curved fuselage surface rather than floating above it, giving it a sloped glass coaming. I'm also fixing the dog's position relative to the cockpit and positioning the pilot's torso correctly within it before writing the full scene code.

Setting up pilot proportions based on the cockpit top height — torso capsule and head sized and placed relative to the cockpit opening, plus goggle lens positioning computed from the head's spherical surface.

Still writing goggle geometry...

Adding ear flaps, goggles positioned to sit proud of the cap edge, and a scarf starting at the neck with a moustache detail. Then I'm placing the dog model with a head sphere and chest capsule positioned relative to the ground height at its z-offset.

For the dog's front paws, I'm checking that they rest just behind the windscreen on the coaming rim — placing small paw spheres with connecting capsules from the chest so they look like they're resting on the edge, verifying the z-positions line up correctly with the windscreen location.

Now I'm figuring out the ears — small scaled spheres angled with a slight rotation to suggest flapping back in the wind, with sign/direction being a minor detail I can adjust later. I'm also adding goggles for the dog, placing lens shapes on the head and generalizing a helper function to compute surface points on any head sphere given center, radius, and offset, so I can reuse it for both the human and dog heads.

Now I'm placing the dog's snout as a box positioned against the head surface, adding a small nose sphere at the tip, and a pink tongue box angled beneath the snout, while skipping mouth lines and eye spots for simplicity. I'm also deciding there's nothing needed for the cowling front hub plate, and moving on to add a landing gear axle.

Skipping the fairing, exhaust, pennants, gravity tank, and propeller for now, I'm considering whether to give the fuselage a cream-colored belly below a certain height threshold, assuming the loft normals handle this correctly. I'm checking the loft function signature to confirm it accepts station arrays with width/height and a bone/color option, and trying to figure out whether the default cross-section is elliptical or if I need to explicitly pass a section type.

I'll leave the sides unspecified and let defaults apply rather than overriding the circle segment count, and I'm setting up paint callbacks for the wing, fuselage, and propeller with appropriately named (and sometimes unused) parameters. Now I'm starting to write the final code file, importing the builder utilities and defining the red and cream color constants for the biplane.

Writing color palette and joint setup...

Worried about typechecking the outline array, I decide to just cast it as a tuple array type rather than importing the type definition to avoid risk.

Now I'm designing the wing geometry as a function, with separate upper and lower wings at different heights and spans, generating each outline procedurally based on half-span and tip-cut parameters.

Setting up the aileron extrusion geometry with symmetric positioning for both wing sides, then starting on the elevator outline shape.

Still defining the stabilizer and fin outlines...

I'll skip the smoothing and mark corners as sharp so the rudder's hinge edge and profile stay crisp, matching where the top meets the fin at y=0.92. For the rudder coloring, I'm considering horizontal stripes in a patriotic red/cream/blue scheme.

Deciding to keep it whimsical with a single yellow rudder instead, using a simple paint function based on vertical position for banding. I'm placing a lathe-based teal spinner near the eye area, then building the prop blade with an extrude shape, orthogonal axes, bevel, and a propeller paint color attached to the prop bone.

Checking the blade's tilt and orientation to make sure the normal and thickness directions line up correctly, then confirming the tip clearance looks right at a 20° tilt. I'm adding a lathed yellow cowling around the fuselage with enough segments for a smooth curve, and now sketching exhaust pipe paths sweeping back from the cowling along each side of the fuselage.

I realize my first exhaust path collides with the lower wing since the pipe's y-position overlaps the wing's thickness range at that x-location, so I'm repositioning the pipes higher, routing them from the cowling along the fuselage side above the lower wing where there's clearance, checking the fuselage's half-width at that point to confirm it still fits against the body.

Now checking the gear placement: the wheel geometry at its current x/z position overlaps the lower wing's leading edge since the wheel's top height exceeds the wing's bottom surface height where their z-ranges intersect, so I need to shift the wheels forward or adjust the wing position to clear this collision.

I need to check whether the gear strut path to the hub clears the lower wing, since the wing occupies that z-range near the fuselage edge, so I should adjust the leg geometry to route around it.

I'm also working out the tire's lathe outline to make sure the lowest point of the wheel polygon sits correctly on the ground given the segment count.

Setting the tail wheel hub similarly with a small sink for floor contact, then positioning the axle rod between the main wheel hubs, checking it clears the cowling bottom. Now I'm building the hubcap shape using a lathe profile for a rounded metal cap.

Now I'm adding the tail wheel strut, fork, and small wheel assembly near the tail, plus a gravity fuel tank sitting on the upper wing as a flattened yellow sphere, and setting up small pennant masts with rods and flag extrusions along the wing.

Alternating red and teal pennant colors for a whimsical look, with the mast reaching about 3.22 total height. I'm adding star roundel decals to the wings and a fuselage decal placed near the nose, checking that each decal's position sits properly on the surface it's targeting.

Now I'm moving to the pilot cockpit setup, building both cockpit positions with cylinders, windscreens, and a headrest sphere scaled to form a fairing mound behind the pilot seat.

I'm checking the capsule and part helper signatures to make sure color and bone options are passed correctly, then sketching out the sphere helmet piece and box snout shapes. I'm also setting up a swept scarf path using a catmull spline for the trailing fabric shape.

Still writing scarf sweep logic...

For the neck, I'm adding a torus ring for the scarf collar wrap, positioning it just below the pilot's head based on the torso and neck height offsets.

I notice the scarf would collide with the tail fin, so I'm shortening it to end closer to the body. Now I'm positioning the waving arm, raising the shoulder-to-elbow-to-hand chain upward above the head with a small glove sphere at the tip.

For the other arm, I'm bending it down so the hand rests on the coaming edge rather than holding a stick, simplifying the pose. I'm also setting the torso as a vertical capsule with a .22 radius and spacing the shoulders out to attach the arm capsules.

I'm shrinking the torso radius to .2 so it sits properly inside the cockpit opening, and planning to add brown leather gloves, a yellow fuselage stripe near the tail, and a "7" number badge as final details before writing the full output.

Writing wing outline function...

Now I'm positioning the roundel decals on the upper and lower wings, projecting them onto the top and bottom surfaces respectively, and placing the eye spheres and pupils on the cowling face.

I'm working out eyebrow placement with capsule shapes and dark coloring, then sketching the smile shape using a curved sweep through a few key points along the face.

Now I'm adding small pink cylinder discs for cheek blush, checking the radius positions line up correctly relative to the face center, and verifying the lathe outline for the flat face disc still makes sense geometrically.

With the geometry settled, I'm finalizing the code: making sure sphere-surface lookups return proper vector types, point arrays work with the catmull-rom and sweep color functions, and all joints get created before export. Then I'll move on to adding accessories like goggles or a hat.
